docs.title: FactHarborDSS
docs.text: Decision Support System · In planning

docs.title: Evidence for better-informed decisions
docs.text:
FactHarborDSS is a planned AI-assisted tool for checking factual claims and, later, comparing courses of action. It would use AI models to assess evidence, and every conclusion would show its sources, reasons and uncertainty, including which steps were AI judgments rather than checks.

It would serve people directly and, through an API with the same functions, software and AI agents acting for a person.

How it would work Principles Cooperate with us

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: AI-assisted analysis can sound convincing without showing what is actually established. A reader needs to see what supports a conclusion, what contradicts it, what is missing and which steps were model judgments.

docs.title: What DSS would offer
docs.text:
• Who it would be for: people who need to check a factual claim before relying on it, such as a statement in the news, a figure in a report or a claim in a document. Stage 1 would start with descriptive claims, such as dates, events and figures, checked against public web sources. Later also people preparing a decision. Software and AI agents acting for a person would use the same functions.
  • What you would do: submit a factual claim. Later you could also describe a decision, with your goals and constraints and the options you are considering.
  • What you would get: a report with a verdict and a separate confidence for each atomic claim, that is, each part of the claim that can be assessed on its own, and, where justified, for the claim as a whole; where no verdict is justified, it says why. It shows the evidence for and against, with exact quotes and their sources, what remains uncertain or missing, what would change the verdict, and which steps were AI judgments rather than checks. For a decision, a later stage would compare the options against your goals and constraints and name the open decisive questions.
  • What stays with you: DSS would not decide for you. In a later stage, any action would need separate authorization and be checked under Evidence-Gated Agents. DSS provides an inspectable basis and saves the evidence it examined, so people can re-examine the assessment later.

How it would work describes the process. DSS follows a few core principles: it supports decisions and does not make them, an assessment is not a fact, only a check verifies, agreement is not a check, and a result never grants permission to act.

docs.title: Planned stages
docs.text:
1. Claim checking: factual claims assessed with public web sources, with the evidence examined saved for reassessment.
  2. Comparative evaluation of assessment quality against independent reviewers.
  3. Decision support for one selected type of decision, using permitted files and human-confirmed goals and constraints.
  4. Controlled actions by AI agents, checked under Evidence-Gated Agents.

Each stage is scoped and authorized separately after the previous one is reviewed; DSS must demonstrate its benefit before routine use.

docs.title: Building on existing work
docs.text:
DSS builds on the FactHarbor application (Alpha): it keeps the Alpha's structure of atomic claims, evidence items and claim assessment boundaries and changes how verdicts are combined—see the Alpha's report walkthrough and what DSS keeps and changes. It also builds on Evidence-Gated Agents: examine what supports a conclusion, and keep permission to share or act separate.

DSS is a project of the FactHarbor association, a Swiss non-profit.

docs.title: Where we are now
docs.text:
Planning stage — 1 November 2026. Stage 1 would check factual claims with public web sources and save the evidence examined. Implementation has not started; DSS benefits have yet to be demonstrated.

Explore the analysis pipeline, the planned architecture, why a fresh implementation, or partnership and funding opportunities.

docs.title: Planned architecture
docs.text:
FactHarborDSS is in planning. The diagrams show the selected design, not an implemented or validated system.

Open the diagram for a larger view. Components show responsibilities, not security isolation. Technical users would call the same application API; the diagram shows the browser path only. Original diagram; repository-wide licensing remains undecided.

docs.title: Core design
docs.text:
• One application: a TypeScript interface served by C#/.NET 10, with a worker initially running in the same process.
  • Traceable evidence: PostgreSQL stores captured web content, source versions, assessments, reports and durable jobs. Full-text search provides the retrieval baseline.
  • Repeatable evidence basis: reassessment uses the saved version without hidden fetching. Refreshes create new versions; model outputs may still differ.
  • Separate source evaluation: Source Reliability has its own service interface and database. Its role in Stage 1 remains undecided.
  • Permissions enforced in code: access, report release and external actions are checked separately. Retrieved documents and AI assessments cannot grant authority; source restrictions also apply to derived reports.

Stage 1 focuses on claim checking with public web sources and saved evidence. From Stage 1 on, technical users such as AI agents acting for a responsible person would get the same functions as people through the same API as the browser interface; confirmations, permissions and approvals stay with people. Broader decision workflows and controlled external actions come later. The pipeline explains the broader assessment and agent-debate design.

docs.title: Core data model
docs.text:
Like the FactHarbor Alpha, DSS splits a claim into atomic claims, statements that can each be assessed on their own, and gives each one its own assessment. The overall assessment builds on these. Assessments cite evidence items that quote exact passages in captured documents, and evidence with a compatible scope can be grouped into claim assessment boundaries. Every judgment records how it was established, and the report names gaps as limitations. The principles set out the rules these records serve.

docs.title: Planning documents
docs.text: How it would work, the principles and the analysis pipeline complement this architecture overview. We supply detailed requirements and acceptance criteria with each agreed piece of work.

docs.title: Association and projects
docs.text:
The FactHarbor association is a Swiss non-profit association (Verein), founded in 2026 and based in Dietlikon, Zürich. Its purpose is to help people make well-grounded decisions and use technology responsibly. Public benefit, openness, independence and transparency guide the work. Public stewardship overview

The association brings together two complementary initiatives. Its FactHarbor initiative develops applications and services for evidence-based decisions, including the existing FactHarbor application (Alpha) and the planned FactHarborDSS. Our AI Charter proposes a trustworthy AI network for free, fair and resilient societies. FactHarborDSS is planned to succeed both the FactHarbor application and the relevant Evidence-Gated Agents core, for claim assessment and decision support.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
These are different projects and maturity levels, not interchangeable names for a delivered system. The overview reflects the project presentation and the DSS planning status as of 1 November 2026.

Work What exists Intended contribution to DSS FactHarbor application (Alpha) An existing claim-checking application with atomic claims, evidence, sources, reasoning, verdicts and separate confidence. Its analysis structure, report structure and the reader's inspection path. Our AI Charter Public framework, commitments, research and articles in draft form; a proposed network. Accountability, openness, traceability and the public-interest context. Evidence-Gated Agents A defined concept and prototype direction; DSS integration remains development work. Examine a proposed step's evidence and authority before permitted release or action. AI Charter Runtime A separate runnable but unfinished proof of concept, exercised with simulated scenarios and local effects. Lessons about controls outside the acting AI. Code reuse remains an explicit choice. FactHarborDSS Published concept, principles, pipeline and architecture overviews; planning continues. A shared core for human and agent claim assessment and decision support. Not yet implemented or evaluated.

The Alpha's reports are concrete examples of an existing application. Charter documents describe principles and proposed structures. The Runtime proof of concept does not establish completed EGA integration, operational certification or DSS security.

docs.title: Continuity without assumed parity
docs.text:
Succeeding the FactHarbor application and the relevant EGA core does not promise delivered feature parity, a replacement date, migration of all historical data or retirement of either predecessor. Stage 1 acquires new web evidence; it does not depend on importing the Alpha's evidence or results.

Read what DSS keeps and changes from the Alpha, Our AI Charter and EGA, and why a fresh implementation is proposed.

docs.title: Our AI Charter and Evidence-Gated Agents
docs.text: Our AI Charter is a public initiative proposing a trustworthy AI network for free, fair and resilient societies. It supplies the wider accountability context for the DSS direction. Its network and assurance structures remain proposals; they are not operational services or certification claims.

docs.title: Five connected pillars
docs.text:
The Charter organizes its work around five pillars:

  1. Accountable AI decisions and actions — evidence, authority and inspectable outcomes for consequential steps. Evidence-Gated Agents is the current focus within this pillar.
  2. Open, plural models — meaningful choice across models, languages and regions.
  3. Data and provenance commons — documented sources, rights, restrictions and access conditions.
  4. Shared assurance and evaluation — independent examination, review, correction and remedy.
  5. Federated public AI infrastructure — independently operated capacity connected through shared rules.

Read the Charter's five-pillar overview. The pillars describe complementary responsibilities, rather than capabilities already implemented in DSS.

docs.title: What an EGA check would do
docs.text:
A working AI proposes an exact next step. The EGA concept examines the evidence for that step, its authority and the applicable access, processing and disclosure permissions. A permitted step proceeds within its checked scope; otherwise it remains stopped with a recorded reason. Authorized human judgment is involved where needed.

Illustration by Robert Schaub and contributors, reproduced unchanged under CC BY-SA 4.0. Original illustration · Source licensing. Open the image for a larger view.

Evidence alone grants no permission. A recommendation, permission to disclose that recommendation and authority to execute an external action are separate. Revisions require a new check where applicable; uncertainty about whether an action occurred requires reconciliation, not automatic repetition.

docs.title: What exists and what remains
docs.text:
The public EGA work defines the concept and prototype direction. The separate AI Charter Runtime is runnable but unfinished, with simulated scenarios and local test effects. Neither establishes a completed DSS integration.

DSS is intended to provide a shared evidence and assessment core for people and AI agents. Stage 1 is narrower: claim checking with public web sources and saved evidence, planned for people and, through an API with the same functions, for AI agents acting for a responsible person. Action integration remains later scope; see the planned architecture.

Explore EGA · Runtime proof of concept · Published articles

docs.title: How FactHarborDSS would work
docs.text:
FactHarborDSS is intended to turn a question into a conclusion whose evidence and reasoning people can inspect.

Use The question it helps answer Check a factual claim What supports or contradicts this claim, and how confident can we be in the assessment? Compare options — later Which course of action is justified by the evidence, given the person's confirmed goals and constraints?

docs.title: From question to an inspectable report
docs.text:
Broader planned approach, not delivered functionality. Additional-agent debate and decision comparison are later scope. Full pipeline and agent roles.

Simplified adaptation of the FactHarbor/DSS design. Attribution: FactHarbor contributors · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Public visual lineage.

A claim is split into atomic claims, statements that can each be assessed on their own. Each atomic claim is assessed with its own evidence and verdict, and the overall verdict builds on the decisive ones.

docs.title: What the reader should gain
docs.text:
• An inspectable basis: the sources and passages actually examined.
  • A reasoned assessment: supporting and contradicting evidence, objections and unresolved gaps, for each atomic claim and overall.
  • An honest result: clear scope, uncertainty and limitations, including when no conclusion is justified.

For decisions, people set the priorities. A recommendation does not itself authorize sharing information or taking action.

The principles set out the commitments behind this, and the home page lists the planned stages.

docs.title: Partnerships and funded development
docs.text:
Help turn the planned FactHarborDSS into a useful tool through practical cases and independent evaluation, or funding and engineering capacity. The FactHarbor association provides the non-profit setting; the existing FactHarbor application (Alpha) offers reports to learn from.

DSS implementation has not started. Stage 1 would assess factual claims with public web sources and save the evidence examined. Comparative evaluation follows separately; file-based decision support comes later.

docs.title: Practical cooperation
docs.text:
For Stage 1, contribute precise factual claims, public sources, independent evidence judgments, or readers willing to assess whether reports are useful. No private file collection is needed.

A later pilot would test one recurring type of decision against agreed goals and constraints, using permitted files and representative cases. Its scope and intended use still need to be selected.

Evaluation should examine evidence gaps, justified conclusions, reader effort, time and cost. These are questions to test, not promised improvements.

docs.title: Funded development
docs.text:
Funding and engineering capacity could support Stage 1 with agreed deliverables:

  • Capture web evidence, preserve it for reassessment, and produce a minimal claim assessment.
  • Check traceability and the reader's ability to inspect sources and reasoning.
  • Report results, limitations and effort to inform the next decision.

Comparative assessment-quality evaluation and the later decision pilot need their own scope and resources. Successful development checks alone do not establish suitability for operational use.

This repository publishes how it would work, the principles, the pipeline and the architecture overview. We supply detailed requirements and acceptance criteria with each agreed piece of work.

Partner introductions, research collaboration, fundraising and clear public communication are also welcome.

docs.title: Start a conversation
docs.text:
Describe the need, who would benefit, and the expertise or resources you could contribute. Use the contact routes, or open a public proposal following the contribution guide.

Scope, success criteria, budget, responsibilities, data use, publication and deployment are agreed for each piece of work before it starts. Keep private evidence and protected evaluation cases or answers out of public messages. Cooperation does not itself authorize processing, publication, deployment or external actions.

No funding target, partner commitment or delivery date is established. Repository-wide licensing and any future application release remain undecided.

docs.title: From FactHarbor to DSS
docs.text: The existing FactHarbor application (Alpha) provides experience to build on. See the FactHarbor report walkthrough, including sources, evidence and separate verdict and confidence labels.

docs.title: What DSS keeps from the Alpha
docs.text:
DSS is designed to keep the Alpha's analysis structure:

  • Atomic claims, each with its own verdict: from 0 (false) to 100 (true), shown in the Alpha as a truth percentage, with seven labels and a separate confidence.
  • Evidence items with the extracted statement, the quoted passage, the source type, whether the item derives from another source, and the scope of its data, such as method, period and region.
  • Claim assessment boundaries that group evidence with a compatible scope, with a finding per boundary where they lead to different conclusions.
  • Search for contradicting evidence, not only for support.
  • Source reliability evaluated by a model, separately from the claim.
  • Challenges by model roles, where only evidence-backed objections change a verdict, and misleading framing explained separately from truth.

DSS would also add a more explicit basis for preserving and replaying the evidence used, and later compare options against human-confirmed goals and constraints. These are design intentions, not delivered capabilities or inherited proof of quality; DSS must demonstrate its own usefulness. The FactHarbor association remains the organization behind both applications.

docs.title: What DSS changes
docs.text:
The Alpha column describes its source code and default configuration as of late October 2026.

Alpha Planned DSS Overall verdict Fixed code combines the claim verdicts, weighting each by centrality, potential harm, confidence, agreement across claim assessment boundaries, whether it carries the input's key truth condition, probative value and share of derivative evidence; where claims point in different directions, a model decides within fixed bounds A labelled model judgment built on the decisive atomic claims, without averaging or counting Evidence before it counts Models rate probative value; code filters out items rated low and items from opinion sources The documentation and origin of each cited item are assessed and shown Evidence weight Probative value and derivative share enter the weighting rules Reasoned weight levels from very strong to very weak, without a formula Minimum evidence With too few items, no directional item, or too little diversity of source types and websites, code sets a claim to unverified A true, mostly true, false or mostly false verdict cites at least one considered item in its direction, or a recorded inference or calculation; no minimum count Repeated runs Code lowers confidence when repeated runs disagree Run variation is kept separate from the verdict and its confidence Source reliability A model rates each source from a search about it, a second model may correct the rating, and code caps it for some source types; its weighting of verdicts is switched off by default Rated from cited third-party material, with insufficient data shown separately and no caps or formulas Derivative evidence Flagged and down-weighted; originals are not fetched, though a claim lacking primary sources may get one extra search Originals of the evidence a verdict rests on are sought within the search allowance

See how it would work, the principles, reasons for a fresh implementation and the planned architecture.

docs.title: Start a conversation
docs.text:
Contact Robert Schaub through LinkedIn or info@factharbor.ch, the contact address published on the FactHarbor overview.

Describe the practical need, contribution or cooperation you have in mind. The partnership and funding page outlines the two main routes. Agree a suitable channel and permissions before sharing confidential material; keep protected evaluation cases and answer keys out of public issues.

docs.title: Analysis pipeline
docs.text:
The planned pipeline connects an exact question to permitted evidence, an assessment people can challenge, and a report released to its intended reader. Claim assessment and decision comparison share evidence and reporting, while using distinct analytical methods.

This is the broader proposed design, not an implemented workflow. Stage 1 covers claim checking with public web sources and saved evidence. Decision comparison and the additional-agent debate route are later scope, subject to evaluation. More agents are not themselves evidence of better results.

Open the diagram for a larger view. The “Conditional agent debate” panel contains possible debate tasks; it does not prescribe all roles, parallel dispatch or a fixed number of model calls. The support assessor is represented in step 4 alongside trusted code checks; both apply on both routes.

Simplified adaptation of the FactHarbor/DSS design. Attribution: FactHarbor contributors · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Public visual lineage.

docs.title: What the agents would contribute
docs.text:
The controller selects only required or justified tasks, their dependencies and their permitted inputs. Each task works against the exact evidence and assessment versions it was assigned.

Task Contribution Advocate Explain the evidence-backed case, including assumptions and limitations; do not defend a preferred answer regardless of evidence. Challenger / specialist Examine counterevidence, alternative explanations, citation or scope defects, or a specific expert question. Self-consistency Examine instability or contradictions on comparable inputs. Repetition and agreement add no independent evidence. Reconciler Accept, reject or retain each material objection as unresolved, with reasons; revise affected findings where justified. Support assessor Judge whether the cited passages support each atomic claim; this remains a model judgment, labelled as one, from a method that must pass independent evaluation before routine use. Trusted code separately checks that references exist, that quotations match the saved text, and typed dates, versions and arithmetic.

These are task roles, not necessarily five permanent agents or five different models. Different role names do not establish independence. Failed or cancelled tasks are reported, not dropped.

docs.title: Challenge without voting or endless retries
docs.text:
The baseline assessment would already examine counterevidence, including a search for contradicting evidence for each atomic claim. When no extra agent is needed, the direct path still undergoes mandatory checks. A required challenge cannot be skipped because another agent agrees. If it cannot run, for example because the budget has run out, it is reported as missing; see gaps, limits and corrections.

Reconciliation follows the substance of an objection, not the number of agents supporting it. A demonstrated reasoning or quotation defect can justify correction without a new source; unsupported disagreement does not automatically lower a verdict or its confidence. Material unresolved issues constrain the conclusion and its intended use.

The controller may refine, ask a person, or return a limited result, hold or stop; further rounds do not reset limits. In a plain fact-check, analytical findings never stop the work or prompt questions; they are named in the report.

docs.title: From candidate to permitted report
docs.text:
Reports retain material objections, dispositions, changes, reasons, uncertainty and stopping conditions—not raw debate transcripts. Only a structurally valid candidate becomes a fixed report edition; in fact-checking it marks any remaining contradictions and excluded evidence. Recipient-specific access, disclosure, quality and any required human review still govern release; a misleading redaction must be withheld.

A report is a basis for decisions, not permission to act. External actions have a separate authorization and execution path and are outside this simplified diagram.

See the principles, the system architecture and how it would work.

docs.title: Why a fresh implementation
docs.text:
The proposed fresh implementation is intended to carry forward the experience and useful work from developing the FactHarbor application while creating a simpler foundation for claim assessment, later decision support and EGA. It starts with a small implementation whose benefits must be verified before the scope expands.

These are development motivations and intended improvements, not measured DSS results. A rewrite alone would establish neither better assessments nor market demand.

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
The maintainer's experience is that the Alpha has accumulated considerable code and complexity, making changes harder to manage. A fresh modular structure is intended to make responsibilities clearer, reduce unnecessary coupling and make changes easier to review.

This does not mean discarding what was learned. DSS keeps the Alpha's analysis structure and changes how verdicts are combined and evidence is weighed; see what DSS keeps and changes. Reusing existing code needs deliberate decisions.

docs.title: Speed and running costs
docs.text:
The intention is to simplify the analysis workflow and avoid unnecessary processing while protecting quality. More steps, agents or model calls are not a measure of better reasoning.

Any improvement must be demonstrated against a suitable baseline, considering assessment quality alongside time, cost and the reader's correction effort. No DSS speedup or cost saving has been established.

docs.title: Quality and testing
docs.text:
Preserving the exact evidence used by each assessment should make comparisons more systematic and regressions easier to detect. The design separates acquisition quality, assessment quality on fixed evidence and the usefulness of the complete reviewer workflow.

Repeatable inputs support investigation; they do not guarantee identical model output or correct conclusions. Independently judged cases, protected evaluation material and explicit acceptance criteria remain necessary.

docs.title: A common foundation for broader capabilities
docs.text:
Fact-checking asks what the evidence supports. Decision support adds human-confirmed goals, alternatives and constraints. EGA also asks whether a proposed step is supported and permitted to proceed.

These uses can share evidence and reporting while keeping their methods and authority boundaries distinct. See how it would work for their purpose and the architecture for the selected foundations.

docs.title: Production readiness
docs.text:
The planned architecture is intended to improve the foundation for database storage, background processing, recovery and access controls, with a path toward more users and workloads. Durable work and explicit permissions should be designed into the application rather than assumed from an AI response.

This is a design direction, not production readiness already achieved. Capacity, recovery, access controls and hosting must be implemented and qualified for their intended use. See the architecture overview.

docs.title: Development with coding agents
docs.text:
Clear requirements, smaller modules, explicit interfaces and focused tests should make delegated changes easier to review and integrate. An accountable integrator, independent review where required and evidence-based acceptance remain necessary.

A better structure may help both human contributors and coding agents. It does not prove faster development, reliable autonomous operation or installed technical enforcement. The contribution guide explains how to propose scoped work.

docs.title: Start small and test the reasons
docs.text:
Stage 1 is bounded claim checking with public web sources and saved evidence. Comparative evaluation follows separately. Continue, narrow or reconsider the work based on demonstrated benefit, not the fact that a rewrite has begun.

The initial work must therefore produce evidence about quality, usefulness and effort as well as functioning software. The cooperation options explain how cases, reviewers, engineering capacity and funding could support that process.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
These principles set out what the planned DSS must and must not do. They are design commitments, not delivered functionality. Which of them Stage 1 covers, and in what form, is set when it is scoped; reports say what was not assessed. The records they refer to are shown in the core data model.

Unless a section says otherwise, its rules apply to all of DSS. A few apply only to fact-checking, that is, to a request that only asks whether claims are true; they are marked Fact-checking only and say what applies in decision support instead.

docs.title: Core principles
docs.text:
1. Support, not decision-making. FactHarborDSS is a decision support system, not a decision-making system. It collects evidence and provides an inspectable information basis to assist people in making decisions; the decisions stay with them. In a later stage, AI agents acting for a person could act only within the authority that person granted, each step checked under Evidence-Gated Agents.
  2. An assessment is not a fact. DSS assesses claims and, later, options, but every verdict and recommendation is labelled as a model judgment and carries no authority.
  3. Only a check verifies. A statement counts as checked only when trusted code or a person has checked it, and a model never gives its own output that status. What has been checked, what lacks essential evidence and what remains a model judgment are always shown separately.
  4. Agreement is not a check. When a model reviews another model's work, or several models or runs agree, the result is still a model judgment.
  5. An authentic source can be about something else. Whether a cited passage concerns the right person or institution, matter, time and relation remains a model judgment until a person checks it. Search can confuse similar records, so a search hit is only a candidate until it has been assessed.
  6. Method quality is not proof in the single case. Measured agreement with independent reviewers describes the method, not an individual verdict. DSS is meant to make human checking faster and more complete, not to replace it, and that benefit must be measured.
  7. Every result shows its basis and its limits. It states how well the evidence supports it, what would change it and what is missing; gaps are named, not hidden.
  8. A result never grants permission. Permission to share or act is given separately and needs its own justification. Urgency never turns uncertainty into knowledge or waives a required check.

The sections below set out how DSS applies these principles.

docs.title: How each result was established
docs.text:
• Each result says how it was established: captured, checked by trusted code (fixed, tested software rules), judged by a model, or reviewed or adopted by a person. Only checks by trusted code or people are called checked, validated or verified, and a model's conclusion is labelled as a model judgment. A person's check is recorded with their role and covers only what they examined.
  • Recorded basis. Each assessment records the reading of the question or claim; for a claim, the context of the statement where known (speaker, date and venue), and for a decision, the confirmed goals, constraints and options; the key details considered, the evidence capture dates, and the versions of the assessment schema and scale.

docs.title: Claim assessment
docs.text: Applies to every factual claim DSS assesses: in fact-checking and as a factual premise of a decision.

docs.title: Results and their meaning
docs.text:
• Atomic claims first. A claim is split into atomic claims; a simple claim is one atomic claim, whose verdict is then also the overall verdict. Each atomic claim gets its own verdict, confidence, reasoning and cited evidence. The overall verdict is a separate judgment built on the atomic claims decisive for it; it never averages their verdicts or counts how many are supported. Where no overall verdict is justified, the report says so and the atomic-claim verdicts stand.
  • Verdict and confidence. A factual verdict is set by model judgment on a scale from 0 (false) to 100 (true), and fixed rules assign its readable label. A separate confidence is explained by the evidence and the completeness of the search. Neither is a calibrated probability, and no formula derives them from weight levels, reliability labels or item counts.
  • Separate states. Mixed is a supported middle result: the evidence shows the claim to be about as much true as false. Unverified means that no adequately supported judgment was reached, for a stated reason: insufficient evidence or an unresolved conflict. A claim that could not be assessed, or an assessment that failed or did not run, is a separate state. Finding no evidence never produces a False or midpoint verdict.
  • Reading and scope. The original wording is kept, and a claim's own qualifiers are neither strengthened nor weakened. Atomic claims that were not assessed are named. Opinions and value judgments get no verdict and are named as not assessable. A literally accurate but misleading claim keeps its factual verdict, and the misleading framing is explained separately.
  • Ambiguous claims Fact-checking only: an ambiguous claim is assessed in its most plausible reading, and the other material readings are named. In decision support, the person clarifies a material ambiguity.
  • Basis and overturn conditions. Each verdict states how well the evidence supports it and names the evidence or finding that would change it. A true, mostly true, false or mostly false verdict on an atomic claim cites at least one considered evidence item in its direction, or a recorded inference or calculation.
  • Decisive atomic claims. A true or mostly true overall verdict requires each atomic claim decisive for it to point the same way: true or mostly true if it supports the claim, false or mostly false if it contradicts it; the reverse holds for false or mostly false overall verdicts. Which atomic claims are decisive is itself a model judgment and is shown in the report.
  • Contradiction notice Fact-checking only: if a verdict still breaks the rule on decisive atomic claims after a correction attempt, it keeps its label but carries a prominent notice naming the decisive atomic claim whose verdict does not point the same way. In decision support, such a result is held until the contradiction is resolved.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Right subject and context. For the atomic claims a verdict rests on, the report shows whether each cited passage concerns the same subject, matter, time and relation, and names open questions.
  • Search in both directions. For each atomic claim, the search also looks for contradicting evidence. Every search query is recorded with its purpose, and the report says whether a search for contradicting evidence ran. A retrieved document is a candidate; it counts as evidence only after it has been assessed.
  • Evidence assessed before it counts. The model first assesses whether each cited document substantiates the statement it is cited for, for example with data, method or checkable sources, and whether it is the original source; a record of what someone said shows that it was said, not that it is true. Material that does not substantiate its statement is not counted as evidence and is named in the report; baseless claims such as fabrications are never considered. For evidence a verdict rests on, the original source is sought within the run's search allowance; if it is not found or not sought, the report says so.
  • Weighed, not counted. Each evidence item gets a reasoned weight level, from very strong to very weak, based on its documentation, origin, independence and the reliability of its source; very weak items are not considered and are named in the report. Items that share an origin count as one basis, not as independent confirmation. The same rules apply to supporting and contradicting evidence. No numeric evidence weights, evidence or source scores, or formulas apply.
  • Scope and claim assessment boundaries. Each evidence item records the scope of its data, such as method, period and region. Evidence with compatible scopes can be grouped into claim assessment boundaries. Where boundaries lead to different conclusions, the assessment shows a finding for each and explains the difference; each atomic claim keeps one verdict.
  • Source reliability. Ratings rest on retrieved, cited third-party material, such as fact-checks, correction records and ownership; without such material the result is insufficient data, not a low rating. Where no evaluation is available, reliability is shown as not assessed. These assessments are shown to readers.

docs.title: Consistency of judgments
docs.text:
• Repeated runs: if runs are repeated on the same captured evidence, a result is never set by picking a favourable run, rerunning until runs agree, or voting or averaging. A single run means stability is not measured. Whether and how run variation is shown is decided after reader testing.
  • Separate measures: evidence sufficiency and any observed run variation stay separate and are never merged into one score. Run variation is also kept apart from the result and its confidence. A model's stated confidence always comes with its evidence-based reasons, is not a calibrated probability and never establishes correctness on its own.

docs.title: Gaps, limits and corrections
docs.text:
• Missing steps: a required task or check that cannot run is named as missing, never silently skipped.
  • Named limits instead of stops Fact-checking only: uncertainty, missing or conflicting evidence, missing steps and atomic claims that could not be assessed are named in the report, and the analysis continues; access, disclosure and release checks still apply. In decision support, such findings can hold the work or limit the result until the person clarifies them.
  • Corrections: an issued report edition is never changed silently. A correction or reassessment creates a new dated edition linked to the earlier one, stating what changed and why; the earlier edition keeps its content and shows that it was superseded.

docs.title: Decisions (later stage)
docs.text:
Applies to comparing options for a decision.

  • People set the basis: goals, constraints and priorities are confirmed by the responsible person.
  • Open points: the report names open decisive points as questions for the person deciding; possible consequences of an error are stated only where evidence supports them.

docs.title: People and software
docs.text: • Same functions through an API: technical users, such as other software and AI agents acting for a responsible person, get the same functions as people, with their own identity and never more rights. Confirming goals and approving actions stay with people.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
• Before routine use: methods must pass independent evaluation against reference judgments by competent reviewers, with pass criteria set before testing. Until then, results are labelled as coming from a method not yet independently evaluated.
  • Independent reference judgments: reviewers record their judgments before seeing DSS results, and disagreements are reported, not forced into consensus. For claims, evaluation covers the reading, the atomic claims and the verdicts, and compares English and German versions of the same claims.

See the analysis pipeline for how these principles fit into the planned workflow.
